overview: Cantia is a Latin name used by Bede for Kent. This card serves both imported labels, but the map’s Cantia outline spreads far beyond the south-eastern kingdom and must not be treated as its verified territory. The Cantia interval of 600 to 800 and Kent interval of 800 to 1000 are map coverage, not the lives of two separate kingdoms. The named sites below are in historical Kent; several institutions continued after royal independence ended.

periods.title: Royal patronage and Christian institutions
periods.summary: Augustine arrived in 597, when Queen Bertha was already Christian. Royal patronage supported Canterbury's new monastery and school.

periods.title: A subordinate West Saxon kingdom
periods.summary: From about 825, Kent, Essex and Sussex formed a subordinate kingdom governed by junior members of the West Saxon dynasty.

periods.title: Institutions after the separate kingdom
periods.summary: Kent's separate kingship ended in 860. Later, Canterbury's monastery underwent reform, while settlement resumed at Lyminge after its earlier abandonment.

items.text: Queen Bertha worshipped at St Martin's before Augustine's arrival in 597. Aethelberht welcomed the mission and gave it land outside Canterbury. Conversion therefore developed through existing relationships, royal decisions and new institutions.

The abbey probably founded in 598 combined churches and a cemetery with gardens, orchards and vineyards. Its school drew monks from far away, connecting learning with the practical support of a resident community.

Textus Roffensis preserves early Kentish laws in a manuscript compiled in the early 1120s. Its survival makes older legal writing accessible, but the date of this copy must be distinguished from the seventh-century rules it transmits.

Aethelberht's law code sets compensation for injuries and property offences, with distinctions among rulers, clergy, free people and enslaved people. It reveals ranked legal categories; it does not prove that every prescribed payment was enforced.

An Old English sample from Aethelberht’s laws reads “Gif feaxfang geweorð ·L· sceatta to bote.” In Christopher Monk’s translation, grabbing someone by the hair calls for compensation of fifty sceattas. The wording survives in a twelfth-century copy of a much earlier code. Hair-pulling even had its own entry in the legal price list.

At Lyminge, a gaming piece was made from a hollow bone cylinder with turned end caps and a bronze rivet. Found in a royal hall setting, it gives tangible evidence of skilled manufacture and play, though the game's exact rules remain unknown.

Broken luxury drinking glass and animal bones accompanied Lyminge's late-sixth- and seventh-century royal complex. Together with the halls and gaming piece, these finds support an interpretation of gatherings organised around feasting and display.

Lyminge's eighth- and ninth-century deposits contain more large marine fish bones, including cod and whiting, than its earlier occupation. The study identifies increasing consumption while warning that recovery methods and different deposits affect comparisons.

Sheep became more prominent in later Lyminge animal remains, while pigs declined. Loomweights, bone needles, pin-beaters and spindle whorls also occur. The researchers suggest increased wool production, but reserve judgment pending fuller analysis of the flocks.

A 741 grant records a fishery on the River Lympne for Lyminge. Written landholding evidence helps explain how an inland religious community could obtain coastal foods; fish bones alone cannot establish a particular fasting rule.

After a raid in 804, Lyminge's community received refuge in Canterbury. Coins, building activity and dated butchered bones show subsequent occupation at Lyminge, challenging the assumption that one recorded attack immediately destroyed the monastery.

By the late ninth century the Lyminge monastery appears to have been abandoned. Sustained military pressure is the researcher's likely explanation. Tenth-century settlement returned under Canterbury's archbishops, showing that the place's history outlasted that institution.

At Canterbury, tenth-century monastic reform organised prayer, reading and manual work. In 978 the abbey's dedication was extended to include Augustine. This later institutional history should not be mistaken for continued Kentish royal independence.

ending.text: Kent entered a subordinate West Saxon kingdom around 825; separate kingship ended in 860. Communities and religious institutions continued, as Canterbury's later reforms and Lyminge's renewed settlement demonstrate.
